claim: Wording a sure option as lives saved versus lives lost flips human choice: about 72% take the sure option in gain wording and 22% in loss wording (T&K 1981, N=152 and 155).
agent_test: Run an Asian-disease-style item set in both wordings through the agent; count answer flips at equal tokens.
audit_note: T&K 1981 text shows N=152 (72%) and N=155 (22% sure-loss option); Data Colada confirms the figures and a replication. Wording note: it is 'sure option', gain vs loss frame.

claim: Human risky-choice framing is real and medium sized: d about 0.5 to 0.6 after bias correction and in Many Labs 1 (earlier uncorrected meta-analyses gave 0.31 to 0.44). It varies a lot by task (d 0.16 to 0.91). Many Labs 1 primary paper: d=0.60 (95% CI .53 to .67) against original 1.13, 86% of 36 samples significant in the same direction, no site heterogeneity (Q(35)=37.01, p=.69).
agent_test: Use d about 0.4-0.6 as the human yardstick; report the agent's flip rate beside it.
audit_note: All figures verified in Kuhberger 2023 and the Many Labs 1 paper (d=1.13 original, Q=37.01 df 35); minor: Many Labs 2 (d=0.40) lies below the stated 0.5-0.6 and is not mentioned, and the 0.44 comes from Pinon & Gambara 2005.

claim: Attribute framing (25% fat versus 75% lean) was the smallest of the three framing types in the Pinon & Gambara (2005) meta-analysis (d=0.26 vs 0.44 for risky and goal framing), and in the food attribute-framing meta-analysis it moved attitudes far more than intentions (d=0.82 vs d=0.05).
agent_test: For a rating-style judge, test whether a wording flip moves the stated score and also whether it moves the final decision.
audit_note: Numbers verified (Pinon & Gambara d=0.260 smallest of risky/attribute/goal; food meta-analysis attitudes 0.82, intentions 0.05 as reported by Kuhberger 2023), but 'smallest framing type in humans' is wider than the sources: Kuhberger reports message framing at only about d=0.10, and Pinon & Gambara compare only three types (1997-2003 studies).
claim_before_audit: Attribute framing (25% fat versus 75% lean) is the smallest framing type in humans (d 0.26) and moves ratings far more than intentions (food meta-analysis: attitudes d 0.82, intentions d 0.05).

claim: Adding 'exactly' to the sure option does not remove the Asian-disease effect: Mandel's null came from about 38 per cell, and a 98-per-cell replication and two later Mandel studies (N=506) found the effect, though small when scored by strict within-person consistency (d 0.17 to 0.20).
agent_test: Compare agent flip rate with and without quantifier disambiguation; do not assume disambiguation alone fixes it.
audit_note: Verified (Mandel & Kapler 2018: N=190 d=0.20, N=316 d=0.17 under the stricter frame-consistency coding, between-groups d=0.50 and 0.34); 'within-person consistency' is a loose gloss for the stricter theory-constrained coding, and the two studies use a financial ADP isomorph with 'exactly'.

claim: Framing effects are not mainly explained by cognitive style, numeracy or age; individual-difference fixes are weak.
agent_test: Do not expect a 'think harder' instruction to cut flips; measure it (compare plain vs extra reasoning).
audit_note: Kuhberger 2023 (citing Wyszynski & Diederich, Peters & Levin, Best & Charness) and Mandel & Kapler 2018 (CRT, numeracy, AOT, NFC not predictive) support it; 'individual-difference fixes are weak' is an inference but follows.

claim: Part of attribute framing works through inference: the chosen frame leaks a reference point, and people who only received the inferred value show the effect anyway (d 0.81 direct, 0.40 yoked). Domain knowledge shrinks it only inside that domain.
agent_test: Compare a neutral restatement that adds the base rate against one that only flips valence.

claim: Preferences depend on the response mode: choice and price of the same gambles disagree (reversal rates 40 to 50%; about 90% of reversals break procedure invariance, not transitivity).
agent_test: Ask for choice and for a score on the same options; flag disagreement in code.
audit_note: Numbers match Slovic 1995 (reversals 40-50%, 10% intransitive, 90% procedure-invariance violations, from Tversky, Slovic & Kahneman 1990), but all supporting lines are that one review (a14/a15/a16 are the same paper) and the LessWrong LLM post lines do not bear on the claim; the original 1990 study was not independently opened.

claim: Base and chat LLMs show human-like gain/loss framing in classic settings: GPT-3 risky choice 45.4% (save) vs 74.1% (die); ChatGPT rated efficacy 5 vs 4 for '70 improved' vs '30 did not' with zero spread over 11 runs each.
agent_test: Run the agent's own model on the same pairs; flip both wording and seed.
audit_note: Jones & Steinhardt Table 9 (45.4 vs 74.1, human 28 vs 78) and Suri et al. (ChatGPT 5 vs 4 in 11/11 runs each) verified; note the GPT-3 figures are means over many save probabilities, not only the classic 1/3 setting, and 'base and chat' rests on one GPT-3 and one ChatGPT study.

claim: LLM framing effect depends on the numbers and the story: near the classic probability it is human-sized, away from it both wordings give the same answer (GPT-3); with narrative context effects are huge and sometimes reversed (Payne 2025), and with purely mathematical statements they vanish.
agent_test: Run the same payoffs in story form and in structured-table form; expect a flip in story only.
audit_note: Jones & Steinhardt (gap near p=1/3, both high above 0.5) and Payne 2025 (sport 85.6%/88.8%, career reversed, abstract math: indifference in 100% of cases for GPT-4o and o3) verified; minor: math test used only two models and at p=0.5 GPT-3 wordings still differed (21.9 vs 46.9).

claim: Frontier and recent open LLMs still contradict themselves across logically equivalent wordings often: 57% to 85% contradictions (GPT-4o, Gemma 2, Llama 3.1), syntactic fragility index 0.52 over 23 models (45.2% of cells high), small US open-source models about 2.2x more fragile than SOTA US (0.81 vs 0.36), and a 40-point admit/reject swing in GPT-4.
agent_test: Report flip rate over paraphrase and polarity (should/should not) variants per model as a gate.
audit_note: Verified: Saeedi et al. 57/74/85%, Elkins & Chun mean SVI 0.52, 45.2% high, US OSS 0.81 vs US SOTA 0.36 (OSS/commercial 2.2x), Echterhoff GPT-4 0.375 vs 0.780; minor: arXiv v1 abstract gave 0.53/0.79, and the four results measure different things (framing contradiction, syntactic endorsement gap, admit/reject rate).

claim: Reasoning helps on bare risky-choice framing but is not a general fix: in 20 LLMs reasoning models are nearly invariant to gain/loss wording and option order (Ge 2026), yet choice-price reversal persists at the top reasoning setting (48.4% to 30.7%), logical-negation consistency is unchanged for GPT-5.4, CoT raised flip rates in 7B models (+13 to +27 points) and scale/CoT did not reliably cut context sensitivity in product choice.
agent_test: Compare plain vs reasoning-on at equal tokens on the same paraphrase set.

claim: In one ChatGPT medicine-rating task, outputs were identical across all 11 runs per frame (5 vs 4), so resampling added no information about the frame effect there; in Elkins & Chun's audit, syntactic fragility did not change significantly when temperature went from 0.7 to 0.0 (mean SVI 0.67 to 0.80, Wilcoxon p=0.875), so it is not simple sampling noise.
agent_test: Show that K samples from one frame all agree; require variation of the frame, not the seed.
audit_note: Suri et al. 11/11 identical ratings and Elkins & Chun's Wilcoxon p=0.875 are right, but the Elkins appendix does not say the check used 3 models, fragility actually rose 16% (0.67 to 0.80) at T=0 (non-significant), and one rating task plus one non-significant ablation does not show that resampling 'cannot' reveal or fix a frame effect.
claim_before_audit: Resampling cannot reveal or fix a frame effect: ChatGPT gave identical ratings in all 11 runs per frame, and Elkins' fragility did not change significantly with temperature (3-model check, p=0.875).

claim: A model-run neutral rewrite before answering removes most of the framing gap in a strong model: GPT-4 admission gap -0.405 to -0.010; Rephrase-and-Respond and System 2 Attention show gains from rewriting the question; but GPT-3.5 overshot (+0.165 to -0.080) and the rewritten text can drift.
agent_test: S1 restatement with code check of numbers and entities versus original; compare answer to answer on original at equal tokens.
audit_note: Echterhoff Table (GPT-4 -0.405 to -0.010; GPT-3.5 +0.165 to -0.080), RaR (64.95 to 89.77) and S2A (62.8 to 80.3) verified; minor: 'overshot' means sign flip at smaller size, Llama-2-13b barely changed, and RaR/S2A are accuracy studies, not framing studies.

claim: DeFrame (answer, rewrite in the opposite frame, write guidelines, self-revise; all model-run) cut framing disparity by 92% in 3B to 14B instruct models on fairness items (BBQ) and was stable on a yes/no decision set; most of the bias drop came from self-revision and guidelines, the opposite-frame step added stability. It does not test code-side reconciliation or gain/loss choice items.
agent_test: Run original, neutral and opposite frame; agree/disagree decided in code; escalate on disagreement.

claim: Generic debiasing instructions and prompt anchors are unreliable: awareness/counterfactual prompts helped some models and hurt others, a debias prompt gave +6.6 points on framing but -21.0 on hyperbolic discounting (CogBias, judgment family), and system prompts or anchors often failed to cut flips. In FRAGILE, CoT, an instruction prompt and CAA steering all raised flips in 7B to 8B models; naming a bias in the prompt can raise it (Yechiam 2026, two models).
agent_test: Do not add 'be unbiased' text; adopt a prompt change only if a held-out paraphrase set improves.
audit_note: CogBias Table 13 (columns checked by arithmetic: 17.7->24.3 framing, 42.8->21.8 hyperbolic discounting) gives framing +6.6, not +5.8 (that is risk compensation), and hyperbolic discounting -21.0, not -13.4 (that is the halo effect); the other parts (Echterhoff awareness/counterfactual mixed, FRAGILE CoT/instruction/CAA raising flips on 7-8B models, Yechiam) check out.
claim_before_audit: Generic debiasing instructions and prompt anchors are unreliable: awareness/counterfactual prompts helped some models and hurt others, a debias prompt gave +5.8 points on framing but -13.4 on hyperbolic discounting, and system prompts or anchors often failed to cut flips. In FRAGILE, CoT, an instruction prompt and CAA steering all raised flips in 7B to 8B models; naming a bias in the prompt can raise it (Yechiam 2026, two models).

claim: Option position and cue words are a second source of answer drift that can be larger than judgment biases (CogBias: first-option choice 77-79% vs 37% chance; direction words 'more/less' push answers and free chain of thought reduces the push). With objective answers (MathComp) a cue word pulls errors toward it (equal cue up to 94%); GPT-4o and Sonnet 3.7 stay under 55% drift except for the indirect-equal cue. In CRTBench, logically heavier rewrites hurt more than passive voice (GPT-5.4-mini: contrapositive 72.4%, double negation 84.6%, passive 98.7%; passive 94-100% across models).
agent_test: Shuffle option order in code and strip direction words; measure flips with and without.
audit_note: CogBias first-option 77.1-79.0% vs 36.8% chance and MathComp (equal cue up to 94%; GPT-4o and Sonnet 3.7 under 55% except Indirect-Equal) check out, but CRTBench's 72.4% (contrapositive) and 84.6% (double negation) are the worst model only (GPT-5.4-mini); other frontier models score about 92-98% on those transformations, so '72% to 85%' is not the range for frontier models.
claim_before_audit: Option position and cue words are a second source of answer drift that can swamp frame effects (first-option choice 77% to 79% vs chance 37%; direction words 'more/less' push answers; free chain of thought reduces the push). With objective answers (MathComp) a cue word pulls errors toward it (equal cue up to 94%); GPT-4o and Sonnet 3.7 stay under 55% drift on most cues. Negation and contrapositive rewrites are a larger drift source than passive-voice rewrites in frontier models (CRTBench: 72% to 85% vs 94% to 100%).

claim: Meaning-preserving prompt format changes alone move accuracy by up to 76 points (LLaMA-2-13B), about 10 points on average, and size, shots or instruction tuning do not remove it.
agent_test: Report spread over several equivalent formats, not one prompt, for every claimed gain.

claim: Value-tinted and time-sliced fact-preserving rewrites flip small open models far more than plain paraphrase (value-tinted 36% to 47% vs paraphrase 18% to 22%), so paraphrase flip rate is a noise floor. FRAGILE's own gap over paraphrase is +0.213 (value-tinted), +0.086 (temporal) and 0.000 (vividness). For frontier models on logic items, surface paraphrase consistency is 94% to 99.7% (CRTBench), so the floor is small there; no frontier floor exists for framed choice items.
agent_test: Report flip rate minus paraphrase-only flip rate.

claim: Part of LLM framing flips reflect information differences between prompts, not pure wording (Wang and Zhang rules differ; Payne frames add story text). A near-matched design (same prospect, polarity swap only) exists for risky choice (Ge 2026, 3 prospects) and for rule-bound decisions (Chun and Elkins: affect adds no drift, h=0.003); none exists for Asian-disease wording in frontier models.
agent_test: Build frame pairs from one structured form so only valence words differ.

claim: Frame effects in LLMs are driven by single tokens and wording statistics (word 'loss' had the biggest Shapley pull; P(stock B) 0.97 vs 0.09), not by loss aversion as a feeling. Across 102 fits of 32 models, pooled loss aversion lambda is only 1.26 (CI 1.06 to 1.46).
agent_test: Token-level ablation of valence words as a cheap screen for restatements.

claim: Persona prompts ('Economist') do not reliably reduce framing effects, and labelling a bias in the prompt may raise it.
agent_test: Compare persona vs plain on the frame-pair set; expect no reliable change.

claim: Foreign-language and fluency manipulations do not give a reliable lever on framing (failed replications, statistical critique).
agent_test: Not worth testing.

claim: Goal and message framing have no consistent effect (d about 0.10 for messages) in the latest review, which conflicts with the 2005 meta-analysis (goal d=0.444).
agent_test: None; low priority for the agent.

claim: Choice-versus-price preference reversal occurs in current frontier models and is only reduced, not removed, by the highest reasoning setting (48.4% to 30.7% choice/price inconsistency, 4 models, 25,920 calls). No test yet of an ask-both-and-compare-in-code check.
agent_test: Elicit a choice and a price for the same two options in separate calls; flag disagreement in code and measure how often it fires with reasoning on and off.

claim: In frontier models surface paraphrase (passive voice) leaves answers stable (94% to 99.7% consistency on logic items), but logically heavier rewrites do not: contrapositive 72.4% and double negation 84.6% for GPT-5.4-mini. A restatement that adds negation is a drift source.
agent_test: Restate neutrally without negation; count answer changes between original and restatement on items with known answers.

claim: When the correct answer is fixed by stated rules, an emotional or evaluative narrative adds no drift in aligned models (Cohen's h=0.003, 8 models, 16,564 valid responses); decisions change only when an admissible fact changes. The frame there carries no information and can be stripped. This was not tested where the frame signals a reference point.
agent_test: Split items into rule-fixed and reference-dependent; strip frame only on the first kind and compare accuracy.

claim: In grounded medical QA (same trial evidence, 6,614 query pairs, 8 LLMs) positive-versus-negative question framing lowers agreement on the evidence direction from 76.2% to 72.0% (beta=-0.219, p<.001), and more so in multi-turn chats (78.4% to 70.7%). Same-frame disagreement of about 24% is the floor.
agent_test: Report framed disagreement minus same-frame disagreement.

claim: Reasoning-mode LLMs are the more frame-invariant class on bare two-option risky choice, and humans sit closer to them than conversational models do on frame and order sensitivity (20 LLMs, 360 humans, 3 base prospects). Reasoning models also move toward expected-value choice.
agent_test: Run the same prospect pairs under both wordings with reasoning on and off; count flips.

claim: A single debias or awareness wording does not carry across bias types: in one benchmark with 3 mid-size models framing improved (+5.8 points) while discounting and financial biases fell (up to -21 points as printed).
agent_test: Test any debias text on held-out item types before enabling it.
